notes.meaning: Two enemy kings, Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel, marched together to attack Jerusalem. Although King Ahaz was an ungodly ruler, God did not permit them to capture the city. The Lord protected Jerusalem so that His promises to David's family and the line of the Messiah would stand.

King Ahaz and his royal court panicked when they learned that Syria had formed an alliance with northern Israel. Their courage melted away, and they shook with terror like trees bending in a severe windstorm. They forgot God's protective promises and saw only the superior numbers of their enemies.

God directed Isaiah to take his son Shear-jashub and go meet King Ahaz along the road by the water reservoir. The boy's name meant 'a remnant will return,' which was a living sign that God would preserve a faithful portion of His people. Ahaz was out inspecting the city's water defenses to get ready for a siege.

Isaiah told the frightened king to calm down, stay quiet, and rest in God's care. The two attacking rulers were like the smoking ends of burned-out firewood, almost finished and lacking real power. God referred to Pekah simply as 'the son of Remaliah' to show contempt for his short-lived human authority.

The allied kings plotted to invade Judah, terrify its people, and carve up the land for themselves. They intended to overthrow David's royal dynasty and set up a puppet ruler called the son of Tabeal. Their wicked scheme went straight against God's everlasting covenant with David.

The Lord God announced that the enemies' scheme would fail and never take place. Earthly kings can make grand military plans, but they cannot overturn what the Lord decrees. Judah's future was secure in God's hands rather than determined by hostile plots.

Syria's power would remain confined to its capital of Damascus, and Rezin would not conquer Judah. In addition, the northern kingdom of Israel would be broken apart and cease to exist as a nation within sixty-five years. That final scattering occurred when foreign kings brought outside settlers to replace the deported Israelites.

Israel's authority was limited to Samaria, and its king had no power to take Jerusalem. God warned Ahaz that if he did not stand firm in faith, he would not stand at all. Real safety comes from trusting God's promises rather than leaning on political schemes.

God offered Ahaz a miraculous sign to prove that Jerusalem would be rescued. The king was free to ask for any miracle he wanted, from the highest heavens to the deepest pit. The Lord graciously gave Ahaz every opportunity to strengthen his weak faith.

Ahaz refused the offer, making the pious excuse that he would not test the Lord. His answer sounded humble, but it was really stubborn rebellion against God's explicit command. He had already resolved to seek help from the pagan empire of Assyria rather than trust God.

Isaiah scolded the royal family for wearing out the patience of God's prophets and now trying God's patience too. By rejecting the offered sign, they treated the Lord's mercy with contempt. Isaiah pointedly said 'my God,' showing that Ahaz was distancing himself from the Lord.

Because Ahaz refused to ask, the Lord promised to give His own great sign to the house of David. A virgin would conceive, give birth to a son, and call Him Immanuel, which means 'God with us.' This ensured that the family of David would survive until the promised Savior was born.

differ.view: The prophecy had an initial partial fulfillment in a child born in Isaiah's day as an immediate token of rescue, and an ultimate, full fulfillment in the virgin birth of Jesus Christ.
The prophecy refers strictly and exclusively to the miraculous virgin birth of Jesus Christ, with no intermediate fulfillment in Isaiah's lifetime.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The original Hebrew word refers to a young woman of childbearing age without asserting virginity, pointing to a natural birth in the royal court during the Syrian crisis.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The sign directly foretells the virginal conception of Jesus Christ by Mary, as reflected in the ancient Greek translation used by the early church.

notes.meaning: The child would grow up eating curds and wild honey until he was old enough to choose good and reject evil. This plain food showed that the child would live a true human life in humble circumstances. It confirmed that normal daily life would continue in the land despite the war.

Before that child grew old enough to tell right from wrong, the lands of both attacking kings would be ruined and abandoned. This gave a clear timeline of just a few years for Judah's relief from Syria and Israel. God fulfilled this quickly when the Assyrian army destroyed Damascus and crippled Samaria.

God warned Ahaz that his stubborn refusal to trust the Lord would bring disaster upon the nation. The Lord would bring the king of Assyria, the very ally Ahaz courted, to overrun Judah. It would bring a time of trouble worse than anything seen since the northern tribes broke away from Judah.

God would whistle to call the armies of Egypt like swarms of biting flies and Assyria like swarms of stinging bees. These two great powers would invade and fight across the territory of Judah. The picture reminds us that even the mightiest foreign armies are completely under God's control.

The invading soldiers would cover the entire landscape, settling in steep valleys, rock caves, and thorn thickets. No corner of the country would escape their reach. Places where desperate people tried to hide would be overrun by the enemy.

The Lord would use the Assyrian empire like a hired razor to shave off Judah's hair and beard completely. In ancient times, forced shaving was an act of severe public shame and total defeat. The foreign ally Ahaz paid with temple treasures would become God's instrument to strip Judah bare.

A survivor in the wasted land would manage to keep only one young cow and two sheep. Because so few people would remain alive, those few animals would have wide open fields and provide plenty of milk and curds for everyone left. An abundance of dairy and honey showed that normal farming had ceased and the population had vanished.

Valuable vineyards that once contained a thousand vines worth a thousand pieces of silver would become overgrown with wild thorns and briers. With the farm workers gone, fertile ground would quickly turn into wasteland. Neglecting God's covenant would turn the richest parts of the land into barren weeds.

People would only be able to enter the overgrown fields carrying bows and arrows. The brush would become so thick and tangled that dangerous wild animals would make their dens there. Places that once fed families would turn into hazardous hunting grounds.

Terraced hillsides that farmers once carefully hoed would be abandoned to weeds and thorns. People would no longer bother climbing the slopes to farm them, so cattle and sheep would simply wander and trample over the ground. God showed that unfaithfulness would reduce their fruitful heritage to unmanaged pasture.
